subject: Encrypted backplane: KEK provisioning and escrow scenarios
messages:
From: Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwood.com>
To: edgeops@acme-corp.com
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-07-05T09:15:00-07:00
Subject: Encrypted backplane: KEK provisioning and escrow scenarios

Hi team,

Thanks for the vendor intake last week — following up with a short design questionnaire and a proposed topology for the encrypted backplane you requested. The goal here is to cover two things: (1) a KEK lifecycle that supports your on-prem HSMs and our cloud-side KMS proxy, and (2) an escrow/escrowless fallback path for operator separation during emergency rotations.

High-level ask from your side: confirm any regulatory constraints that would prevent us from holding an encrypted KEK blob in your VPC (zero plaintext, wrapped with your HSM pubkey) and validate the allowed out-of-band escrow holder (third-party or customer-only).

Attached: acme-encrypted-backplane-arch.svg (topology), rotation-test-plan-ACME.pdf (test steps), kms-secret-handling-cheatsheet.md (ops notes).

Proposal summary: 
- Primary KEK stored only as wrapped blobs in Acme VPC vault. Redwood runtime will request wrapped KEK via VPC peering/VPN to a local KMS proxy and unwrap inside your HSM enclave during bootstraps.
- Operator separation: we recommend a 3-party escrow model (Acme HSM, Redwood split-witness, optional external escrow) where no single party can produce plaintext KEK alone.
- Rotation cadence: quarterly rolling rotations with staggered windows per-region to avoid simultaneous cache invalidations. Detailed timeline in rotation-test-plan-ACME.pdf.

Open questions for Acme (please reply inline):
1) Do you require HSM attestation reports pushed to your auditors, or is pulling attestation from your HSM acceptable?
2) Any prohibition on outbound HTTPS to Redwood control-plane endpoints for rotation coordination (we can use pull-based WebSocket if needed)?
3) Preferred escrow provider (listed in the doc) or customer-managed only?

Next steps: once you confirm constraints, Karthik will schedule a 30-min topology review with your EdgeOps and Security teams.

Best,
Connor
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Encrypted backplane: KEK provisioning and escrow scenarios

Connor — thanks, useful summary. A few initial clarifications from our security team: 

- We cannot accept any escrow model where a vendor retains a material (even if wrapped) that would enable unwrapping offsite without our explicit multi-sig. Any Redwood-held component must be strictly split and auditable.
- Attestation: we require SHA-256 attestation reports to be pushed to our S3 evidence bucket after each ceremony and for every HSM firmware update. Pulling is acceptable only for ephemeral read-only checks.
- Egress: outbound HTTPS to a Redwood control plane is allowed only to a specific CIDR range and on port 443; we need to see the IP ranges. If that's not possible we will accept an SFTP push of rotation-ready blobs to our locked bucket.

Also noted a question about downtime: what is the expected window for a KEK rotation if both sides perform staggered switchover? Please include worst-case rollback steps.

We attached a short checklist (see inline) and will take Karthik up on the review.

Thanks,
EdgeOps (on behalf of Acme Security)

Subject: Re: Encrypted backplane: KEK provisioning and escrow scenarios

Hi — replying with concrete options and tradeoffs so we can lock to one approach during the topology review. Long version below; TL;DR choices: (A) Customer-only escrow (zero Redwood capability) or (B) Split-witness escrow (Redwood holds a non-reconstructible share + customer HSM share).

Option A — Customer-only (highest control, more ops):
- KEs (KEK-encrypting-keys) are generated and wrapped entirely inside customer HSM. Redwood only stores the wrapped blob and never receives any unwrapped material.
- Rotation: customer signals rotation by replacing wrapped KEK in the agreed S3 bucket/locked path. Redwood runtime will validate signatures and fetch the new wrapped blob on restart.
- Pros: compliance-friendly. Cons: requires scheduled downtime for runtime restarts or heavy engineering for live in-memory swap.

Option B — Split-witness via asymmetric escrow (balanced):
- Implement a threshold mechanism where Redwood generates an ephemeral share that is cryptographically useless alone (e.g., sealed via customer HSM pubkey + HW-backed attestation). Customer holds HSM share. To reconstruct, both shares and a documented ceremony are required.
- Rotation can be orchestrated rolling with near-zero traffic impact using prefix caching and staggered route drain; worst-case rollback documented in rotation-test-plan-ACME.pdf (section 3).
- We propose quarterly rotations, with emergency out-of-band rotational path that uses a time-limited unseal token delivered to a pre-registered Ops mailbox and audited via the attestation logs.

Attestation / Evidence:
- We can push SHA-256 attestation bundles to your S3 after each ceremony (automated): this satisfies the push requirement. IP ranges for Redwood control-plane egress will be provided in an SLA appendix.

Downtime / Rollback notes:
- Planned rolling rotation (Option B): typical rolling window 10–25 minutes per shard depending on sequence length distribution; worst-case full cluster rollback 90 minutes if a rollback trigger is needed.
- If you pick Option A and require zero restarts, we will scope engineering work for live-key-swap which adds ~4 weeks of effort.

Action items for the review call:
- Connor: share the annotated diagram with the proposed subnet/CIDR mapping.
- Marissa: prepare the runbook excerpt for the ceremony and assign two Redwood on-call delegates.
- Acme: confirm if external escrow provider is acceptable or only customer-hosted.

Connor/Marissa/Olga will coordinate times; proposing Tue Jul 13 10:00 PDT for a 30-min review.

Cheers,
Karthik
Director, Trust & Infrastructure
Redwood Inference
